THE  NEW  EDITION  OF  THE 

Genuine  "Oxford"  Teachers'  Bible. 

WITH   ILLUSTRATIONS. 
The  Most  Complete  Biblical  Compilation  of  the  Nineteenth  Century. 


With  New  Helps  and  a 
Magnificent  New  Series  of 
Maps. 

Specially  prepared 
to  illustrate  the  geo- 
graphy of  Palestine 
and  adjacent  coun- 
tries, from  the  earliest 
times  to  the  destruc- 
tion of  Jerusalem,  and 
embodying  the  most 
recent  discoveries 
down  to  March,  1895. 


EEVISED  throughout  by 
the  Soundest  Biblical 
Authorities  in  Accordance 
with  the  Most  Eecont  In- 
vestigations. 

Possession  of  this 
will  obviate  the  neces 
sity  of  a  number  of 
books,  while  it  will 
concentrate  the  mind 
of  the  student  on  his 
work. 


COMPRISING 

Compendiotis  and  Exhaustive  Information  on  all  points  of  Biblical 
Study,  Analytical,  Critical,  Chronological,  Historical  and  Geo- 
graphical; A  Glossary  of  Antiquities ;  A  Dictionary  of  Proper 
Names  and  Subjects ;  A  Concordance,  and  a  New  Indexed  Atlas 
and  Maps  ;  Sixty -four  full-page  plates,  being  Authentic  Reproduc- 
tions of  Documents,  Monuments  and  Contemporary  Portraits, 
Illustrating  the  History  of  the  Old  and  New  Testaments. 

This  well-known  volume  in  Us  present  form  has  lost  nothing  of  its  former  util- 
ity, but  is  further  enriched  with  new  authentic  information  of  every  description, 
arranged  with  the  closest  attention  to  facility  of  reference.  Thus  enlarged,  the 
book  has  become  by  far  the  most  instructive  and  exhaustive  compendium  of  every 
kind  of  information  essential  to  Biblical  study. 

THE    ILLUSTRATIONS. 

The  Illustrations  form  a  distinctive  feature  of  the  new  edition,  and  present  a 
novel  and  valuable  departure,  never  before  attempted  in  works  of  this  description 
on  a  scale  so  full  and  complete.  They  have  been  selected  and  described  by  E. 
Maunde  Thompson,  D.  C.  LM  LL.  D.,  Principal  Librarian  of  the  British  Museum; 
A.  S.  Murray,  LL.  D.,  F.  S.  A.,  Keeper  of  Greek  and  Roman  Antiquities,  British 
Museum;  and  E.  A.  Wallis  Budge,  Litt  D.,  F.  S.  A.,  Acting  Assistant-Keeper  of 
Egyptian  and  Assyrian  Antiquities,  British  Museum.  Special  care  has  been  taken 
to  insert  only  authentic  copies  of  objects  which  bear  upon  matters  recorded  in 
Holy  Scripture.  To  each  illustration  is  added  a  short  description,  supplying  dates 
and  facts. 


This  New  Edition  is  also  supplied  without  the  Illustrations.

Grand  Rapids  Mich. :  GENTLEMEN — Re- 
ferring to  your  letter  of  March  zd,  in  re- 
ference to  the  chairs  placed  in  our  hall. 
We  have,  so  far,  had  no  occasion  to  find 
anything  but  satisfaction  with  the  goods 
which  you  have  placed  in  our  hall.  The 
automatic  hinge  is  exceptionally  valuable, 
and  its  working  is  thoroughly  practical, 
and,  as  we  believe,  bound  to  be  durable. 
We  have  had  a  number  of  inquiries  in 
reference  to  the  place  where  we  bought 
these  chairs,  and  we  are  always  glad  to 
say  a  good  word  for  them.  We  regret, 
however,  that  we  allowed  so  many  of  the 
i8-in.  chairs  to  be  placed.  The  only  com- 
plaints we  have  had  have  been  from  people 
who  have  felt  that  they  were  cramped  for 
room.  Hoping  that  you  may  have  a  large 
sale  for  your  goods,  I  remain,  yours  truly, 
Fred.  8.  Goodman,  Secy.

ASSOCIATION   BUILDING,    OTTUMWA,    IA. 

OCCUPIED  JANUARY  20,  1892. 
Dimensions,  69x87  feet.  Cost,  $36,000.  Population,  16,000. 


STATEMENT    REGARDING    THE    WOEK    OF    THE 
INTERNATIONAL    COMMITTEE. 


Following  the  instructions  of  the  Indianapolis  Convention,  the  Com- 
mittee has  administered  the  wide  work  intrusted  to  it  in  all  its  depart- 
ments, on  both  the  home  and  foreign  field,  with  careful  reference  to  the 
means  and  resources  provided  by  the  Associations  and  their  friends. 

I. — The  monthly  meetings  of  the  Committee  have  been  regularly  held, 
at  which  the  sub-committees  on  Finance,  the  General  Work,  the  College, 
Kailroad,  German,  Physical,  Educational,  and  Office  and  Publication 
Departments,  and  on  the  Foreign  Work,  have  submitted  reports  and 
recommendations  concerning  the  work  and  future  movements  of  the 
Committee's  secretaries.  The  meetings  of  the  Committee  and  of  the  sub- 
committees have  been  attended  by  the  general  and  office  secretaries,  to 
whom  has  been  referred  the  detail  work  necessitated  by  the  action  there 
taken. 

The  resignations  of  Messrs.  William  H.  Sage  and  George  F.  Peabody, 
as  members  of  the  Committee,  were  reluctantly  accepted,  and  Mr.  Charles 
F.  Cox,  of  New  York,  was  elected  to  fill  one  of  the  vacancies  last  October. 

A  conference  of  the  Committee  and  its  secretaries  was  held  in  New 
York,  September  12-17,  1893,  in  which  all  departments  of  the  interna- 
tional work  were  carefully  considered.  By  this  means  the  comprehensive 
administration  of  the  work  by  the  Committee  and  its  intelligent  prosecu- 
tion by  the  secretaries  were  effectively  promoted. 

II. — The  Board  of  Trustees  held  its  annual  meeting  March  13,  1894, 
in  New  York.  Mr.  Jonathan  N.  Harris  positively  declining  re-election, 
Mr.  Samuel  Colgate  was  chosen  president,  and  Mr.  John  S.  Bussing  was 
re-elected  treasurer. 

The  treasurer  received  on  April  9,  1894,  from  the  heirs  of  the  estate  of 
Mr.  Sidney  Dillon,  a  fund  of  $25,000,  to  be  known  as  "The  Sidney  Dillon 
Fund,"  the  income  of  which  is  to  be  applied  toward  the  support  of  Rail- 
road Departments  organized  at  points  on  the  lines  of  the  Union  Pacific 
Railway  system  among  its  employees.  Mr.  Dillon  took  a  deep  interest 
in  the  welfare  of  railroad  employees,  especially  on  the  Union  Pacific 
road,  with  the  management  of  which  he  was  so  long  connected.  His 
knowledge  of  the  railroad  department  of  the  Association  as  it  existed 


10 

x>n  that  road  led  him  warmly  to  approve  of  it,  and  his  intention  to  be- 
queath a  fund  in  aid  of  it,  though  not  expressed  in  his  will,  had  been 
made  known  to  his  heirs — Mrs.  Peter  B.  Wyckoff,  Mrs.  G.  S.  Moulton, 
and  Messrs.  Sidney  Dillon  Bipley  and  Harry  Dillon  Kipley — who  have 
most  generously  united  in  the  gift  of  this  fund  bearing  the  name  of  Mr. 
Dillon  and  devoted  to  the  welfare  of  railroad  employees. 

HI.—  1.  By  the  courtesy  of  Mr.  J.  J.  Me  Williams,  of  Buffalo,  and  at 
his  home,  a  parlor  conference  of  friends  of  the  Committee  was  held  on 
November  14,  1893. 

The  aonual  dinner  meeting  of  the  Committee,  with  its  secretaries  and 
friends,  was  held  in  New  York,  November  23,  1893. 

At  the  invitation  of  the  St.  Louis  Association,  members,  secretaries  and 
friends  of  the  Committee  were  entertained  at  a  dinner  in  that  city  Decem- 
ber 5,  1893. 

At  all  these  meetings  the  international  work  was  fully  presented,  and 
the  satisfaction  expressed  by  the  many  friends  present  served  to  confirm 
the  Committee  in  its  estimate  of  the  great  value  of  such  meetings. 

2.  The  Association  exhibit  at  the  Columbian  Exposition  attracted  very 
general  notice.  The  portion  relating  to  the  educational  department 
received  high  commendation,  and  the  whole  exhibit  was  ranked  among 
those  worthy  of  special  mention  and  attention. 

A  program  was  prepared  for  the  World's  Congress  of  the  Associa- 
tions, which  was  held  on  Association  Day,  October  6th,  in  the  Memorial 
Art  Palace,  Chicago.  Important  papers  were  read  and  addresses 
made  by  Elbert  B.  Monroe,  Chairman  of  the  International  Committee, 
Lord  Kinnaird,  President  John  M.  Coulter  of  Lake  Forest  University, 
William  E.  Dodge,  Cephas  Brainerd,  C.  M.  Hobbs,  of  Denver,  E.  L. 
Shuey,  of  Dayton,  and  L.  D.  Wishard. 

IV. — At  33  State  and  Provincial  Conventions  during  1893  the  Com- 
mittee was  represented  by  its  own  members  and  secretaries,  and  by  lead- 
ing friends  of  the  work.  A  total  of  5,803  delegates  from  980  Associations 
attended  these  conventions,  bringing  report  concerning  a  work  for  young 
men  full  of  promise.  In  almost  every  instance  ample  provision  for  the 
State  work  of  the  coming  year  was  made  by  the  delegates.  This  was  often 
unexpected,  owing  to  the  general  financial  stringency  prevailing  through- 
out the  country. 

V. — Following  the  instructions  of  the  Indianapolis  Convention,  the 
committee  has  issued  credentials  to  delegates  to  the  World's  Conference 
to  be  held  in  London  June  1-7.  Appropriate  observance  has  also  been 
promoted  in  this  country  of  the  Jubilee  (June  6)  of  the  parent  London 
Association,  and  a  call  has  been  issued  to  all  the  Associations  to  commem- 
orate this  anniversary  with  some  suitable  semi-centennial  observance. 
In  connection  with  such  services  it  has  been  recommended,  at  the  sug- 
gestion of  various  friends,  that  contributions  be  made  by  the  Associa- 
tions and  those  interested  in  their  labors  toward  a  permanent  fund  in 
support  of  the  work  of  supervision  and  extension  entrusted  by  the  Con- 
ventions to  the  International  Committee. 


11 

As  a  tribute  to  Mr.  George  Williams,  the  honored  founder  of  the 
iJondon  Association,  an  appropriate  memorial  address  has  been  pre- 
pared for  presentation  to  him  on  Jubilee  Day,  in  the  name  of  the 
Associations  of  North  America,  and  signed  by  the  members,  trustees  and 
secretaries  of  the  International  Committee  and  by  the  chairmen  and  sec- 
retaries of  the  State  and  Provincial  Committees. 


VI. — TERRITORIAL  ADMINISTRATION. 

1.  In  the  South  and  Southwest. — The  members  of  the  Committee  in  the 
South  and  Southwest  have  co-operated  effectively  with  the  secretaries 
assigned  to  those  sections — H.  P.  Andersen,  with  headquarters  at  Atlanta, 
and  Cecil  L.  Gates,  at  Kansas  City. 

(1)  The  State  organizations  have  been  strengthened.   Mr.  Andersen,  early 
in  1893,  at  the  request  and  with  the  co-operation  of  the  State  Committee, 
prepared  for  and  aided  in  conducting  the  Georgia  Convention.     He  also 
arranged  for  the  securing  of  W.  M.  Lewis  as  the  State  Secretary  of  both 
Georgia  and  South  Carolina.     To  Alabama  ami  Mississippi  he  rendered  a 
similar  service  in  arranging  for  F.  L.  Willis  as  their  State  Secretary. 
For  Tennessee,  in  its  time  of  emergency  last  fall,  at  the  request  of  its 
State  Committee  he  arranged  for  and  attended  the  State  Convention,  and 
by  timely  visitation  conserved  the  work  in  the  whole  State. 

Mr.  Andersen  has  also  rendered  valuable  aid  to  the  local  organizations 
at  Augusta,  Atlanta,  Athens  and  Rome,  Ga. ;  Greensboro  and  Asheville, 
N.  C. ;  Memphis  and  Chattanooga,  Tenn. ;  Mt.  Sterling,  Ky.,  and  at 
several  other  points.  He  has  attended  thirteen  meetings  of  State  Com- 
mittees, the  State  Conventions  of  Georgia,  Virginia,  South  Carolina, 
North  Carolina,  Alabama  and  Mississippi,  besides  several  district  and 
secretarial  conferences.  Throughout  the  Southeast  Mr.  Andersen's  work 
has  been  effective  and  helpful. 

(2)  Mr.  Gates  after  useful  visitation  last  spring  in  Colorado,  at  Salt  Lake 
City  and  at  the  City  of  Mexico,  spent  considerable  time  in  Nebraska, 
Idaho,  Kansas  and  Arkansas  in  aiding  local  and  Railroad  Associations. 
In  Kansas  effective  work  was  done  at  many  points  preliminary  to  the 
State  Convention. 

In  October  Mr.  Gates  was  assigned  specially  to  the  Southwest,  with 
headquarters  at  Kansas  City,  and  since  then  has  rendered  important  ser- 
vice on  that  field,  and  has  served  temporarily  as  acting  State  Secretary  of 
Missouri.  The  work  of  the  whole  year  has  required  of  him  114  visits  to 
52  towns  in  17  States ;  22  meetings  of  state  and  local  committees,  and 
boards  of  directors ;  51  public  addresses ;  attendance  at  the  State  Con- 
ventions of  Ohio,  Kansas,  Missouri  and  Texas,  and  138  important  inter- 
views with  officers  and  leaders  in  the  work  and  in  railroad  management. 

Ten  Associations  in  four  Southern  States  were  aided  by  T.  K.  Cree  last 
Spring,  including  a  protracted  building  fund  canvass  in  Augusta,  Ga. 

(3)  Among  young  colored  men  an  excellent  and  effective  work  has  been 
accomplished  by  the  Committee's  Secretary  in  that   important  field, 
William  A.  Hunton. 

Two  useful  conferences  have  been  planned  and  conducted  by  him,  one 
for  Virginia  and  North  Carolina  at  Norfolk  and  the  other  for  College  Asso- 
ciations at  Nashville,  both  being  well  attended. 


12 

Mr.  Hunton  has  also  made  useful  visits  to  fourteen  colored  Associations 
in  as  many  cities,  and  to  three  points  where  the  work  is  not  yet  organ- 
ized. 185  days  were  spent  by  him  in  conference  with  Association  officers 
and  in  giving  the  aid  needed  at  these  points,  much  help  being  in  the  line 
of  financial  solicitation  for  the  necessary  expenses  of  the  local  work.  Self- 
support  of  existing  Associations  in  this  field  is  yet  very  difficult.  The 
rapid  formation  of  new  organizations  is  not  therefore  encouraged  until  a 
better  development  of  existing  work  is  assured.  Substantial  progress 
has,  however,  been  made  the  past  year,  and  new  Associations  were  or- 
ganized at  Kittrell,  N.  C.,  Memphis  and  Little  Kock;  also  at  Pittsburgh, 
Pa.,  and  at  New  Haven,  Conn.  • 

To  20  College  Associations  Mr.  Hunton  made  24  visits,  occupying  45 
days,  and  resulting  in  improved  methods  of  work,  an  increase  of  Bible 
classes,  and  many  conversions.  His  visitation  has  extended  into  14  States. 

2.  In  the  West  and  Northwest.— (1}  While  C.  K.  Ober  has  given  counsel 
and  help  to  both  Mr.  Andersen  and  Mr.  Gates  upon  their  fields,  he  has  been 
chiefly  occupied  in  the  West  and  Northwest,  with  headquarters  at  Chicago, 
whither  he  removed  from  Kansas  City  after  he  had  arranged  for  Mr. 
Gates  to  succeed  him  there.  His  work  has,  therefore,  comprised  develop- 
ment of  the  work  in  the  Southwest,  in  which  he  was  succeeded  by  Mr. 
Gates  ;  co-operation  with  Mr.  Andersen  in  the  South  and  the  taking  up  of 
work  in  the  West  and  Northwest,  with  residence  at  Chicago.  He  has 
visited  points  of  greatest  need  in  Nebraska,  the  Dakotas,  Minnesota  and 
Manitoba ;  attending  conventions  in  Iowa  and  Michigan,  and  correspond- 
ing and  counseling  with  State  committees  and  workers  in  Ohio,  Indiana, 
Illinois  and  Wisconsin. 

Mr.  Ober  has  also  visited  the  Santee  Indian  Agency  in  Nebraska,  and 
with  the  co-operation  of  Mr.  Cochran,  the  Vice- Chairman  of  the  Inter- 
national Committee,  has  conducted  negotiations  with  Indian  Associations 
and  secured  contributions  from  their  friends,  which  give  promise  of 
enabling  the  Committee  soon  to  place  in  the  field  a  competent  Indian 
Secretary  for  work  among  young  men  of  his  own  race. 

To  bring  deliverance  to  city  Associations  in  financial  distress  for 
current  expenses  or  building  funds  has  for  years  been  a  very  serious 
problem.  The  raising  of  money  for  the  relief  of  such  Associations  by 
International  and  State  Secretaries  has  made  their  lives  a  burden  and 
has  overtaxed  their  time,  which  ought  rather  to  be  given  to  the 
supervision  for  which  they  are  specially  trained  and  set  apart,  and 
which  if  neglected  by  them  will  not  be  done.  As  experiments  looking 
toward  the  solution  of  this  problem  Messrs.  Ober  and  Weidensall  have 
recently  arranged  for  a  financial  work  by  W.  E.  Lougee,  at  Hastings, 
Neb.,  and  East  Saginaw,  Mich.,  on  a  plan  which  in  both  places  has 
proved  entirely  satisfactory  to  the  brethren  there  and  at  whose  expense 
the  experiments  were  made.  "A  fit  man  "  is  the  factor  indispensable  to 
the  success  of  this  Association  life-saving  service.  In  answer  to  prayer 
and  effort,  it  is  hoped  that  such  men  will  be  raised  up  to  supply  this 
urgent  need  of  the  Associations. 

(2)  Kobert  Weidensall  has  effectively  co-operated  in  the  Western  work, 
attended  the  Illinois  and  Nebraska  Conventions,  and  the  Western  Secre- 
tarial Institute.  He  has  also  made  many  public  addresses,  and  has 


13 

specially  aided  in  Nebraska  the  Lincoln  and  Hastings  Associations  in 
time  of  financial  difficulty. 

(3)  Henry  E.  Brown  participated  in  the  Bible  work  of  the  Illinois  Con- 
vention and  of  the  Western  Secretarial  Institute,  and  visited  fourteen 
places  in  three  Western  States.     Mr.  Brown's  varied  and  useful  career  as 
a  secretary  of  the  Committee,  as  stated  in  the  report  presented  to  the 
Indianapolis  Convention,  closed  December  31st. 

(4)  John  E.  Hague  also  devoted  considerable  time  to  this  field,  aiding 
local  Associations  and  State  Committees.     The  resignation  of  Mr.  Hague 
was  accepted  September  1st  with  deep  regret.     He  carries  with  him  into 
the  church  work  which  he  has  undertaken  the  brotherly  sympathy  of  all 
who  have  been  associated  with  him  during  his  many  years  of  fruitful 
effort  in  Christ's  name  among  young  men. 

3.  In  the  East  and  Canada. — The  Eastern  and  Middle  States,  in  which 
many  of  the  stronger  State  organizations  are  found,  have  been  visited  as 
occasion  arose  by  Messrs.  Morse,  Cree,  and  other  secretaries  located  in 
New  York  city.  Mr.  Hague  also  spent  considerable  time  in  New  Eng- 
land, where,  among  other  duties,  he  represented  the  Committee  at  the 
Maine  Convention.  He  also  visited  four  points  in  New  Jersey  and  Penn- 
sylvania. In  addition  to  a  representative  of  the  college  work,  Mr.  Cree 
attended  the  convention  in  New  Hampshire,  Mr.  Morse  in  Massachusetts, 
and  Mr.  Wishard  in  Vermont. 

The  convention  of  the  Maritime  Provinces  last  Summer  was  attended 
by  T.  K.  Cree  and  George  A.  Hall,  and  that  for  the  Pacific  Northwest, 
held  at  Victoria,  B.  C.,  by  F.  B.  Pratt,  C.  J.  Hicks  and  W.  H.  Williams. 
In  both  cases  neighboring  Associations  were  visited  and  encouraged. 
The  Ontario  Convention  was  attended  by  Mr.  Morse,  who  sought  at  the 
same  time  to  render  aid  to  the  Toronto  Association.  Mr.  Cree  has  since 
spent  ten  days  with  the  same  Association. 

H.  E.  Brown  participated  in  the  Canadian  Northwest  Convention  at 
Winnipeg,  and  visited  ten  villages  in  Manitoba,  holding  meetings  for  the 
promotion  of  Bible  study  and  active  Christian  work  among  young  men. 

VII.— THE  EXTENSION  FUND. 

The  time  and  efforts  of  S.  A.  Taggart  have  been  divided  between 
.  attention  to  Extension  Work  and  co-operation  in  the  general  work  of  the 
Committee.  In  promoting  the  work  of  special  extension  by  the  organiza- 
tion of  Extension  Fund  Committees,  and  advising  concerning  their 
methods,  he  has  visited  41  Associations,  chiefly  in  the  Eastern  and 
Middle  States,  addressing  meetings  of  members  and  counseling  with 
officers  and  committees.  A  number  of  these  places  have  been  visited 
more  than  once.  He  has  also  attended  the  State  Conventions  of  Penn- 
sylvania, Arkansas  and  Minnesota,  and  two  district  conferences. 

The  Extension  Work  can  be  easily  undertaken  and  as  easily  abandoned 
by  an  Association.  Wherever  competent  management  can  be  secured, 
especially  in  the  person  of  one  capable  and  interested  leader  upon  the 
Extension  Fund  Committee,  the  work  promotes  systematic  giving  among 
our  members  and  intelligent  interest  in  the  growth  of  work  for  young 
men  at  home  and  abroad.  The  progress  made  by  such  Associations  as 
have  been  blessed  with  such  leadership  ought  to  awaken  earnest  prayer 


14 

and  inquiry  to  discover  in  every  Association  this  needed  worker  and 
organizer. 

VIII. — DEPABTMENTAL  WOBK. 

1.  In  the  College  Department  John  B.  Mott's  work  may  be  outlined  as 
follows : 

(1)  Visitation.    Forty-four  College  Associations  were  visited,  and  eight 
city  Associations  in  twenty-one  States  and  two  provinces. 

(2)  Organization.    Assistance  was  rendered  in  perfecting  organizations 
at  three  points. 

(3)  Conventions.    In  order  to  insure  a  more  thorough  supervision  of  the 
college  field,  Mr.  Mott  has  spent  fully  five  months  in  attending  conven- 
tions and  conferences  and  in  preparation  therefor.      The  list  includes 
two  summer  schools,  two  deputation  conferences,  five  presidential  con- 
ferences, four  State  conventions,  one  International  Convention,  five  con- 
ferences of  secretaries,  one  missionary  conference  and  the  students'  con- 
gress of  the  World's  Columbian  Exposition. 

(4)  Correspondence.    Owing  to  the  fact  that  during  a  part  of  the  year 
there  was  no  secretary  devoting  his  entire  attention  to  the  office  depart- 
ment of  the  college  work,  much  more  time  than  usual  was  spent  in  look- 
ing after  the  steadily  increasing  volume  of  correspondence. 

(5)  Matters  Receiving  Special  Attention.     More  time  than  ever  has  been 
devoted  by  Mr.  Mott,  as  Chairman  of  its  Executive  Committee,  to  the 
Students  Volunteer  Movement.     This  movement  has  made  more  sub- 
stantial progress  during  this  year  than  during  any  year  since  its  organ- 
ization. 

Special  prayer  and  attention  have  also  been  given  to  the  promotion  of 
spiritual  awakenings  in  the  colleges.  Many  others  have  co-operated  very 
earnestly.  It  is  gratifying  to  note  that  several  hundred  more  college  men 
have  been  led  through  this  special  effort  to  accept  Christ  than  during  any 
preceding  year  in  the  history  of  the  College  Associations. 

In  visitation  a  great  deal  of  time  has  been  spent  in  State  universities. 
Further  careful  attention  to  this  exceedingly  important  part  of  the 
college  field  will  be  amply  repaid  by  even  more  blessed  results  than  have 
yet  been  experienced. 

2.  F.  S.  Brockman  has  engaged  in  extensive  visitation  touching  the 
colleges  and  attending  the  State  Conventions  in  nearly  every  Southern 
State.     83  visits  were  made  to  67  institutions,  and  five  new  Associations 
were  formed.    He  has  also  attended  two  summer  schools,  the  International 
Convention  and  secretaries'  conference,  and  a  deputation  and  a  presiden- 
tial conference. 

3.  Logan  Herbert  Boots  has  visited  colleges  in  seven  States,  and  con- 
ducted two  college  conferences  on  the  Pacific  Coast.     He  also  attended 
the  summer  schools,  the  Alabama  Convention,  and  the  Western  Deputa- 
tion Conference.    His  engagement  as  a  secretary  of  the  Committee  expired 
September  1,  1893,  but  since  that  time  he  has  represented  the  Committee 
at  the  New  England  State  Conventions  and  visited  several  Associations. 

4.  E.  Lawrence  Hunt  has  visited  the  Pacific  Slope,  giving  most  atten- 
tion to  such  leading  institutions  as  the  University  of  California  and 


15 

Stanford  University,  organizing  three  Associations  and  participating  in  a- 
college  conference. 

5.  As  representatives  of  the  Committee,  John  L.  Marshall,  Jr. ,  spent  a 
month  among  the  Kansas  colleges  ;  W.  H.  Sallmon  visited  the  Maritime 
Provinces  and  conducted  a  students'  conference,  and  Gilbert  A.  Beaver 
attended  the  New  England  presidential  conference. 

2.  The  Railroad  Department  has  taken  most  of  the  time  of  C.  J.  Hicks 
during  the  year.     Since  June  1st  he  has  been  assisted  in  this  work  by 
E.   L.   Hamilton.      The  depression  in  railroad  business   has  rendered 
impossible  any  marked  extension,  although  new  Associations  have  been 
opened  at  Gladstone  and  Clifton  Forge,  Va.,  where  the  Chesapeake  & 
Ohio  Kailway  Company  has  erected  new  Association  buildings,  and  at 
Watertown,  N.  Y. ,  where  a  secretary  has  been  placed  on  the  pay-roll  of 
the  Company. 

The  Directors  of  the  Chesapeake  &  Ohio  Railway  have  contributed 
$2,000  for  an  Association  library  to  be  located  at  Clifton  Forge  for  the 
use  of  Association  members  along  the  line  of  the  road.  Much  care  has 
been  taken  in  the  selection  of  this  library,  and  its  catalogue  has  been 
placed  on  the  list  of  publications  sold  by  the  Committee  as  a  model  list 
for  Railroad  Associations. 

A  thorough  visitation  of  all  the  Railroad  Associations  in  the  West,  and 
of  many  in  the  East,  has  been  made.  The  year  has  in  many  respects 
tested  the  quality  and  standing  of  the  Railroad  Department,  as  railroad 
officials  have  been  forced  to  reduce  expenses  wherever  possible.  Espe- 
cially has  this  been  the  case  where  receivers  have  been  appointed  to 
manage  the  roads.  But  in  spite  of  these  demands  for  economical  ad- 
ministration, but  few  reductions  have  been  made  in  the  appropriations 
granted  for  the  support  of  this  work,  and  but  a  single  Association  (North 
La  Crosse,  Wis.)  has  closed  its  doors.  Much  time  has  been  required  of 
the  Railroad  Secretaries  of  the  Committee  in  acquainting  new  officials 
and  receivers  with  the  basis  and  character  of  the  Railroad  Association 
work. 

March  29-April  1  the  Seventh  International  Railroad  Conference  was 
held  in  the  Railroad  Men's  Building,  New  York  City.  This  was  the 
largest  and  most  helpful  Railroad  Conference  thus  far  held,  over  three 
hundred  delegates  being  in  attendance. 

The  opening  of  a  new  $50,000  building  by  the  Pennsylvania  Railroad 
Department  of  Philadelphia,  and  of  a  large  addition  doubling  the  former 
capacity  of  the  Railroad  Men's  Building  in  New  York  City,  are  two  of  the 
most  encouraging  items  of  the  year. 

The  railroad  committee  has  been  greatly  helped  in  the  administration 
of  its  work  by  its  new  chairman,  Charles  F.  Cox,  Vice-President  of  the 
Canada  Southern  Railway. 

3.  Mr.  Olandt's  attention  has  been  given  chiefly  to  the  internal  develop- 
ment of  existing  German  branches,  including  aid  in  several  important 
building  movements,  and  efforts  to  secure  and  train  desirable  secretaries 
and  physical  directors. 

4.  Mr.  Hodge,  in  caring  for  the  Educational  Department,  has  given  the 
valuable  aid  and  counsel  of  an  expert  to  directors,  educational  commit- 
tees and  secretaries  at  58  points  in  11  States.     He  has  successfully  pro- 


16 

moted  educational  exhibits  at  the  International  and  several  State  Conven- 
tions. He  made  or  collected  a  large  part  of  the  admirable  Association 
exhibit  at  the  Columbian  Exposition.  These  practical  object  lessons 
have  done  more  for  the  useful  growth  of  the  educational  work  than 
months  of  discussion.  Mr.  Hodge  has  also  prepared  the  Committee's 
valuable  pamphlet,  No.  656,  on  "Educational  Class  Work." 

Among  encouraging  results  may  be  mentioned  :  (1),  100  associations  are 
making  more  intelligent  study  of  the  needs  of  the  young  men  in  their 
communities,  in  order  to  better  adapt  their  educational  classes  to  such 
needs  ;  (2),  industrial  art  education,  shop  work  and  instruction  in  lines 
of  practical  science  and  in  mechanical  and  architectural  drawing  are 
offered  by  a  growing  number  of  Associations ;  (3),  endowments  of  their 
educational  departments  have  been  given  to  several  Associations  ;  (4),  the 
.securing  of  systematic  courses  in  mechanical  and  architectural  drawing 
and  other  forms  of  industrial  work  by  25  Associations,  through  the  co- 
operation of  the  Pratt  Institute,  will  greatly  promote  a  uniform,  higher 
standard  of  work  ;  (5),  educational  work  has  been  given  far  more  promi- 
nence at  conferences  and  conventions  than  ever  before. 

5.  Physical  Department  work  has  been  carried  on  under  the  leadership 
of  Dr.  Gulick  on  the  same  lines  as  in  previous  years.  A  growing  number 
of  Associations  receive  counsel  and  help  regarding  this  department,  and 
several  State  Committees  are  looking  after  it  with  intelligence  and  vigor. 
Indoor  athletic  contests  are  the  chief  new  feature.  George  W.  Ehler, 
of  Chicago,  has  kindly  consented  to  superintend  interstate  work  between 
Illinois,  Missouri,  Iowa,  Indiana  and  Michigan,  without  expense  to  the 
Committee. 


IX.— THE  CENTRAL  OFFICE. 

The  secretaries  who  spend  most  of  their  time  at  the  office  have  been 
fully  occupied  with  the  correspondence,  including  that  relating  to 
finances,  secretarial  work  and  building  movements  ;  preparation  of  pub- 
lications ;  and  consultation  with  visitors,  who  come  on  all  sorts  of  errands. 
The  growth  of  the  work  in  the  field  steadily  increases  that  which  must 
be  done  in  the  office.  Twenty-two  new  pamphlets  and  leaflets  have  been 
issued. 

The  resignation  of  Curtis  M.  Thorpe,  who  for  ten  years  had  ren- 
dered a  very  efficient  service  in  connection  with  many  business  details, 
was  reluctantly  accepted  in  October.  His  position  is  filled  by  George  L. 
Leonard. 

The  Historical  Library  now  contains  2,094  volumes  in  twenty-one  lan- 
guages. 197  Association  periodicals  were  received  during  1893. 

The  Day  and  Week  of  Prayer  were  widely  observed  last  November, 
.owing  in  part  to  extended  effort  by  the  Committee  and  its  secretaries. 
More  than  ever  it  is  becoming  a  season  of  spiritual  blessing  throughout 
the  brotherhood.  This  is  realized  the  present  year  to  an  unusual  extent 
by  the  College  Associations. 

In  aid  of  the  international  work,  565  Associations  took  up  collections 
.aggregating  $6,857.97.

X. — THE  FOREIGN  WOBK. 

This  naturally  divides  itself  into  the  work  on  the  foreign  field  and 
the  administration  of  the  Foreign  Department  at  the  office  of  the 
Committee. 

1.  The  Foreign  Field.     (1.)  Japan.     The  year  closed  with  30  Associa- 
tions, 15  of  them  being  composed  of  students.    Four  city  Associations 
employ  Japanese  general  secretaries.     A  building — the  gift  of  a  business 
man  in  America — costing  $2,000,  was  erected  in  Kyoto  during  the  year 
for  the  Association  in  the  government  college.     The  building  of  the 
Tokyo  Association   was   nearly  completed.      The   summer  school  was 
attended  by  600  students,  being  the  largest  gathering  of  Christian  stu- 
dents ever  held,  excepting  the  Student  Missionary  Volunteer  conventions 
in  America.     Messrs.  Swift  and  Miller  reached  the  end  of  their  busiest 
year  greatly  encouraged  by  the  results  of  the  work. 

(2.)  India.  The  number  of  Associations  in  India  at  the  close  of  the 
year  was  80,  five  of  which  are  composed  of  students.  One  new  building 
was  secured.  The  Week  of  Prayer  was  observed  in  Madras  with  excellent 
results.  Mr.  McConaughy  reports  the  conversion  of  ten  associate  mem- 
bers during  the  year.  Mr.  and  Mrs.  J.  Campbell  White  sailed  for  Calcutta 
in  September,  arriving  early  in  December.  He  has  already  established 
an  Association  composed  of  young  business  men,  and  has  been  warmly 
welcomed  by  the  missionaries,  business  men  and  the  Indian  Christians. 

(3. )  Brazil.  Myron  A.  Clark,  after  eighteen  months  of  successful  study 
of  the  language,  chose  Rio  de  Janeiro  as  the  headquarters  and  point  of  de- 
parture for  the  Association  movement  in  Brazil.  An  Association  has  been 
organized,  which  has  maintained  its  existence  in  spite  of  the  demoralized 
condition  of  the  city  during  the  recent  war. 

(4. )  Fields  without  secretaries.  Favorable  reports  have  been  received 
concerning  the  Associations  in  China,  Ceylon,  Persia,  Asia  Minor,  Syria 
and  European  Turkey.  The  first  College  Association  in  South  America 
has  recently  been  organized  in  the  International  Institute,  Santiago, 
Chili.  An  urgent  appeal  has  been  received  from  the  missionaries  of 
Cheefoo,  in  North  China,  for  a  secretary. 

2.  The  Administration  of  the  Foreign  Department  of  the  Committee  has  re- 
quired of  Mr.  Wishard  :  (1),  extensive  tours  among  Associations  and  con- 
ventions to  promote  the  support  of  the  foreign  work  ;   (2),  search  for  suit- 
able secretaries  for  the  fields  to  which  missionaries  have  called  men; 
(3),  public  presentation  of  the  facts  of  the  foreign  movement  in  leading 
churches,  before  church  clubs  and  various  Christian  conventions  ;    (4), 
increase  of  the  supporters  of  the  work ;   (5),  conference  with  the  foreign 
committee  concerning  important  matters  submitted  to  the  Committee  by 
the  secretaries  on  the  field  ;  (6),  correspondence  in  connection  with  the 
foregoing  lines  of  work. 

RICHARD  C.  MOESE, 

General  Secretary.

TABLE  III.-CITY  AND  TOWN  ASSOCIATIONS. 

COMPILED  FROM  OFFICIAL  REPORTS  RECEIVED  BY  THE  INTERNATIONAL  COMMITTEE  BETWEEN 
JANUARY  15  AND  MARCH  15,  1894. 

The  names  of  officers  are  the  most  recent  that  have  come  to  the  knowledge  of  the  Committee,  as 
far  as  convenience  of  printing  permits  their  insertion. 

Some  Associations  prefer  to  report  for  their  official  years,  closing  at  various  dates,  bat,  for  the 
most  part,  the  reports  are  for  the  calender  year,  1893 ;  a  number,  from  Associations  recently  organ- 
ized  or  re  organized,  are  necessarily  incomplete.

WORK 


IN  THB  WEST,  CONSISTING  OF 


I,  The  Young  Men's  Christian  Association  Training  School, 

CHICAGO,      ILL. 

Established  and  Incorporated  in  June,  1889,  endorsed  as  an  INTERNATIONAL 
TRAINING  SCHOOL  by  the  International  Convention,  at 
their  meeting  in  Kansas  City,  May,  1891. 

OBJECT. 

To  train  young  men  for  tbe  duties  of  General  Secretaryship,  Physical  Directorship  and 
other  Association  offices. 

COURSES   OF    STUDY. 

The  complete  courses  cover  two  years,  and  comprise  in  both  Secretarial  and  Physical 
Departments :  First,  a  thorough  and  systematic  course  of  theoretical  studies,  covering  every 
phase  of  Association  work  ;  Second,  a  practical  training,  each  student  being  assigned  to 
regular  duties  in  one  of  the  nine  departments  of  the  City  Association  ;  Thirrt,  a  comprehen- 
sive study  of  the  Bible,  and  how  to  use  and  teach  it;  Fourth,  training  in  the  conduct  of  the 
BJBLW,  TRAINING  CLASS,  and  how  to  do  PKKSONAL  W'OKK  ;  Fifth, 
daily  instructions  in  gymnastics  ;  Sixth,  courses  of  special  lectures 
on  Christian  Sociology,  work  in  the  Educational  Department  and 
general  topics  closely  allied  to  Association  work. 

UNSURPASSED   EQUIPMENT. 

The  school  is  now  located  in  the  elegant  new  Central  Building 
of  the  Chicago  Association,  where  it  has  the  free  use  of  ample 
class  rooms,  good  library  facilities  and  the  finest  Association 
Physical  Department  on  this  continent.  This  will  greatly  add  to 
the  efficiency  of  thescbool  an«i  gives  it  model  facilities  for  tbe 
training  of  men  for  Association  work. 

CALENDAR.-FiFTH  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

FALL   TERM.— Begins   Wednesday  morning,    September    12th, 

1894. 

WINTER  TERM  —Begins  Thursday  morning,  January  3d,  1895. 
SPRING  TERM.— Begins  Monday  morning,  April  1st,  1895. 

ESTIMATED  COST  FOR  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

Tuition,  $50;  Living  Expenses  for  the  School  Year,  including 
Board,  Room,  Association  Membership,  Gymnasium  Suit, 
Laundry,  Text  Books  aud  attendance  upon  Convention,  estimated 
at  $225  to  $300. 

OFFICERS  AND  PRINCIPALS.

E.  L.  HA7 FORD,  M.D.,  Con.  SKCKETAKY.    H.  M.  STARKEY,  M.D.,  Rtc.  SECRETARY.

DIVIDENDS  NEVER  EQUALLED  BY  THOSE  OF  ANY  OTHER  COMPANY, 


It   will   pay    YOU    to   investigate. 


The  late  Rev.  Henry  Ward  Bcecher  said,  in  ansiver  to  an 
anxious  inquirer  : — "A  wise  Life  Insurance  of  $5,000  or  $10,000, 
payable  at  the  death  of  the  insurer,  does  not  benefit  his  wife  and  children 
only  after  his  death,  but  it  is  of  great  use  to  the  man  himself.  It  tends 
to  make  him  economical,  methodical  and- frugal  in  his  expenditures,  cuts 
off  many  indulgences  which  would  waste  his  means,  and  gives  quiet  to 
his  mind  in  business  troubles  and  especially  in  sickness  and  in  prospect 
of  death.  He  does  not  look  in  anguish  on  the  prospect  of  his  family 
at  his  death  loaded  with  the  expense  of  his  sickness,  funeraj  expenses, 
&c. ,  and  thrown  upon  the  world  without  means  of  livelihood,  at  a  time 
when  grief  will  go  far  to  paralyze  their  energies. 

Take  out,  then,  young  man,  a  good  policy  in  a  sound  Life  Insurance 
Co. ,  a  non-forfeitable  policy,  as  large  as  you  can  afford,  and  as  years  roll 
on  thank  God  that,  should  you  die,  your  family  will  not  fall  into  the  bit- 
ter woes  of  poverty."

CAST-STEEL  WORKS 


OF 


FRIED.  KRUPP, 


ESSEN,    GERMANY. 


AMERICAN    OFFICE: 

15  GOLD  ST.,  NEW  YORK. 


.    O.    13031,    3B-7B. 


Represented  by  THOMAS  PROSSER  &  SON. 


These  Works  cover  an  area  of  1,200  acres,  employ  about  18,000  men, 
have  the  most  improved  plant,  and  stand  unique,  from  the  fact  that  they 
have  their  own  Ore  and  Coal  Mines,  Blast  Furnaces,  etc. ,  and  that  every 
stage  of  manufacture  is  under  their  own  supervision,  and  are  not  (like 
others)  dependent  on  the  open  market  for  a  miscellaneous  assortment  of 
crude  material,  which,  in  connection  with  75  years'  experience,  enables 
them  to  turn  out  a  product  of  a  very  superior  quality,  second  to  none,  and 
at  the  same  time  the  different  grades  of  Steel  are  always  of  the  same 
uniform  quality.
